extra.message: The HTTP request path (self.path) is appended directly to the server working directory on line 14 (path += self.path) and then read with open(path).read() on line 22. The only protection is a weak regex filter on line 10 evaluated with re.match on line 11, which only blocks the exact sequence /../../ at the start of the path. Attackers can bypass it with ../, URL-encoded sequences, or other traversal variants to read arbitrary files from the server. The path should be normalized and confined to a safe base directory.

extra.message: The post_id value is concatenated directly into the SQL query string on line 70 ('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ' + post_id) and passed to conn.execute(). The only guard is a regex on line 67 evaluated with re.match on line 68; because the regex is compiled with re.MULTILINE the start/end anchors match per line, so a payload such as a number followed by a newline and extra SQL passes the check and is injected into the statement, enabling SQL injection. Use parameterized queries as in main_safe.py.

The user-supplied url request parameter (request.args.get('url') on line 13) is fetched server-side via urllib.request.urlopen(url) on line 15. The only validation is url.startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com') on line 14, which is trivially bypassable with values such as https://insecurewebapp.com.evil.com or https://insecurewebapp.com@evil.com, allowing SSRF to arbitrary internal or external hosts. Restrict destinations by parsing and allowlisting the hostname.

TLS certificate hostname verification is disabled on line 6 (context.check_hostname = False). This makes the client accept certificates issued for any hostname, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks. Keep the default (check_hostname = True) and validate certificates properly.

The username value, derived from the user-controlled session_id cookie via self.decrypt() on lines 15-20, is written into the HTML response without escaping on line 37 (Hello %s formatted with username). Because the cookie is decrypted with AES-CBC using an attacker-controlled IV and no message authentication (line 20), an attacker can tamper with the ciphertext to control the decrypted username and inject HTML/JavaScript, causing XSS. HTML-encode the output and use authenticated encryption for the cookie.

The session_id cookie is decrypted with AES-CBC on line 20 using an IV read from the user-supplied cookie (lines 16-17) and without any MAC/authentication of the ciphertext. This allows an attacker to tamper with the cookie via bit-flipping and enables padding-oracle attacks, breaking session integrity. Use authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM or encrypt-then-MAC.

extra.message: When a username cookie is present, the server calls Username.pickle() on line 14, which (per the comments on lines 15-19) deserializes the user-controlled cookie via pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(cookies.get('username').value)). Deserializing untrusted data with pickle enables remote code execution. Do not use pickle for untrusted input; use JSON with schema validation or a signed token.

The payment signature on line 13 is computed as SHA-256 of (secret + payment_information) (line 12). Using a Merkle-Damgard hash in the construction H(secret || message) is vulnerable to hash length-extension attacks, allowing an attacker who observes a valid signed message to forge a valid signature for an extended message (e.g., to tamper with payment parameters) without knowing the secret. Use HMAC instead.
